items.title: Effective Commit Messages
items.body:
# Writing Effective Commit Messages

## Format
```
type(scope): subject

body

footer
```

## Types
- **feat**: New feature
- **fix**: Bug fix
- **docs**: Documentation only
- **style**: Code style changes (formatting, no logic change)
- **refactor**: Code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature
- **test**: Adding or updating tests
- **chore**: Maintenance tasks

## Example
```
feat(auth): Add OAuth2 login support

Implement OAuth2 authentication flow using authorization code grant.
Adds login button and callback handler.

Closes #123
```

## Best Practices
1. Use imperative mood ("Add feature" not "Added feature")
2. Keep subject line under 50 characters
3. Separate subject from body with blank line
4. Wrap body at 72 characters
5. Explain what and why, not how

items.title: Git Branch Strategy
items.body:
# Git Branch Strategy

## Branch Types

### Main Branches
- **main**: Production-ready code
- **develop**: Integration branch for features

### Supporting Branches
- **feature/***: New features (branch from develop)
- **bugfix/***: Bug fixes (branch from develop)
- **hotfix/***: Urgent production fixes (branch from main)
- **release/***: Release preparation (branch from develop)

## Workflow

### Starting a Feature
```bash
git checkout develop
git pull origin develop
git checkout -b feature/user-authentication
```

### Finishing a Feature
```bash
git checkout develop
git merge --no-ff feature/user-authentication
git branch -d feature/user-authentication
git push origin develop
```

### Hotfix Process
```bash
git checkout main
git checkout -b hotfix/security-patch
# Make fixes
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff hotfix/security-patch
git tag -a v1.0.1
git checkout develop
git merge --no-ff hotfix/security-patch
git branch -d hotfix/security-patch
```

## Best Practices
1. Never commit directly to main or develop
2. Use pull requests for code review
3. Delete branches after merging
4. Keep branches short-lived (< 1 week)
5. Rebase feature branches before merging

items.title: Git Conflict Resolution
items.body:
# Git Conflict Resolution

## Understanding Conflicts
Conflicts occur when Git cannot automatically merge changes from different branches.

## Conflict Markers
```
<<<<<<< HEAD
Your changes
=======
Their changes
>>>>>>> branch-name
```

## Resolution Steps

### 1. Identify Conflicts
```bash
git status
# Shows files with conflicts
```

### 2. Open Conflicted Files
Look for conflict markers (<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>)

### 3. Resolve Conflicts
- Review both versions
- Edit file to keep desired changes
- Remove conflict markers
- Test the resolution

### 4. Mark as Resolved
```bash
git add <resolved-file>
```

### 5. Complete the Merge
```bash
git commit
# Or for rebase:
git rebase --continue
```

## Prevention Strategies
1. **Pull frequently**: Stay in sync with the main branch
2. **Small commits**: Easier to identify and resolve conflicts
3. **Communicate**: Coordinate on files being edited
4. **Feature toggles**: Avoid long-lived branches

## Tools
- `git mergetool`: Launch visual merge tool
- VS Code: Built-in conflict resolution UI
- GitKraken, SourceTree: Visual conflict resolution

## Aborting
If things go wrong:
```bash
# Abort merge
git merge --abort

# Abort rebase
git rebase --abort
```
